name: Railay Beach
label: Railay Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ao Phra Nang' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Ao Nang Cliff View Resort' (pois).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Railay Beach'.
notes: Limestone-cliff peninsula beach reached only by boat.

text.description:
Railay is a small peninsula between Krabi town and Ao Nang, cut off from the mainland by high limestone cliffs, so you can only reach it by boat. For photographs, the best-known spot is Ao Phra Nang. Pale sand and calm water sit right up against tall cliffs, with a small island, Ko Rang Nok, just offshore and longtail boats moving about nearby. Guides often call it the most photographed beach in the Railay area, and it is easy to see why: the cliffs, sand, sea and island give you several layers in one frame.

Railay's cliffs draw rock climbers from around the world, and the area has been a popular beach destination in Krabi since tourism began there in the 1970s. Ao Phra Nang is one of its four main areas, alongside West Railay, East Railay and Ton Sai.

Stand mid-beach on the sand and face the cliffs and the islet. Keep the horizon level using your gridlines, and let a longtail boat or a person on the sand give the scene some scale. Go early if you can: the light reaches the cliffs before about 9 AM and the beach is quieter. If you are up for a scramble, a route through boulders at the southern end leads to a gap in the cliff with a shallow pool and the sea framed between rock walls.
text.geographic_location: Ao Phra Nang is one of the four main areas of Railay, in Krabi province between Krabi town and Ao Nang. It is reached by a trail from East Railay.
text.directions_text: Railay has no road access, so head first to Ao Nang or Krabi town and take a boat from there. Boats from Krabi dock at East Railay, and Ao Nang is about 15 minutes by longtail boat from Railay. From the southern end of the East Railay boardwalk, a public trail runs under overhanging limestone cliffs to Phra Nang Beach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the cliffs, sand and sea together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Ko Rang Nok or a longtail boat.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (mid-beach on the sand, facing the limestone cliffs and the islet offshore). White sand and water framed by towering limestone cliffs, with a small island offshore (Ko Rang Nok) and longtail boats nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on a lower line so the cliffs fill the upper part of the frame. Put a boat or a person in the foreground or midground for scale. For a quieter alternative to the beach-level shot, the Bat Cave opening frames Phra Nang Beach and Ko Rang Nok, and Railay Viewpoint gives a wide panorama. Both involve steep, slippery climbs that guides say become dangerous after rain, so wear proper footwear.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cliffs to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sand does not turn the sky and sea pale. Try Live Photos or a short burst when boats pass, so you can pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 9 AM, when the light hits the cliffs and the crowds are thin.

text.access_note: Ao Phra Nang is reached by boat plus a public trail from East Railay; check with your boat operator for current boat and access details before you go.

name: Ao Nang
label: Ao Nang Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ao Nang Viewpoint' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Ao Nang Landmark' (pois).

notes: Main beach resort town of Krabi with a sunset promenade.

text.description: Ao Nang is a resort town on the Krabi coast, and this spot is about seeing the whole of it at once. From the Ao Nang Viewpoint you look down on the Ao Nang area, with limestone mountains behind and the sea and beaches stacked in layers below. That is an overview you cannot get from the sand. The town is one of the ten subdistricts of Mueang Krabi District. It consists chiefly of a main street of restaurants, pubs and shops aimed at tourists, and long-tail boats run from the main beach to other beaches and nearby islands. You may spot a few of those boats from above. The viewpoint is a roadside lookout on the road between Ao Nang and Nopparat Thara, about 500 m before Nopparat Thara, and it has roadside parking. One guide calls it the best viewpoint in the Ao Nang area, and it is described as free to visit. Sunset, roughly 5:30 to 6:30 p.m., is the suggested time. For the classic close-up frame, Ao Nang Beach has the sand and rocks in the foreground with the limestone mountain rising behind. Nopparat Thara Beach is a quieter alternative, with a sand bridge and small island at low tide. Check access to the viewpoint locally before you set out.
text.geographic_location: Ao Nang is in Mueang Krabi District, on the coast of Krabi province. The viewpoint sits on the road between Ao Nang and Nopparat Thara, a short way before Nopparat Thara.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed nearby, so head along the road from Ao Nang towards Nopparat Thara. The viewpoint is about 500 m before Nopparat Thara, with roadside parking. Some guides describe a walk to reach a viewpoint here, so ask your hotel or a local to confirm where to stop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in as much of the mountains, beaches and sea as you can. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the limestone peaks or the boats on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ao Nang Viewpoint (roadside lookout on the road between Ao Nang and Nopparat Thara, about 500 m before Nopparat Thara; roadside parking). An elevated view of the whole Ao Nang area, with limestone mountains behind and the sea and beaches stacked in layers below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line. Let the beaches and the water fill the layers, with the mountains as the backdrop. If you want the classic beach-and-rocks frame instead, Ao Nang Beach is the alternative, and Nopparat Thara Beach is a quieter one.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or sky to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours stay rich. Try a panorama for the full sweep, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, about 5:30–6:30 p.m., is the suggested time. Arrive a little earlier to find a spot and try a few frames as the light changes.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is a roadside lookout described as free to visit, so check access locally before you go.

name: Tiger Cave Temple
label: Tiger Cave Temple
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6710654: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Hilltop temple reached by about 1,260 steps with views over Krabi.

text.description: Tiger Cave Temple (Wat Tham Suea) is a Buddhist meditation temple in the forested Kiriwong Valley, north-north-east of Krabi town. It is known for the tiger paw prints in the cave, the tall Buddha statues and the long climb to the top. The temple dates back to 1975, when a monk went to meditate in the cave and saw tigers roaming around it, which gave the place its name. The stairway to the summit now has 1,260 steps, and the top sits at 278 metres. A large golden Buddha stands up there, and from the shrine you can see the temple buildings and much of Krabi town. For photographs, the temple works at two scales. Down in the grounds, the rainforest, old trees and surrounding mountains make a good backdrop. Higher up, the golden statue and the wide view over the town give you the classic frame. Monkeys live on the lower stairs and around the grounds, so they may well wander into your pictures. Keep a respectful distance and let them get on with their day. Take your time on the stairs, because some risers are over 30 cm high. Stop to shoot on the way up rather than at the top only, when you are tired. Carry water and keep your phone in a pocket or wrist strap on the climb. Check the official site before you go for anything about access.
text.geographic_location: Tiger Cave Temple is in the forested Kiriwong Valley, north-north-east of Krabi town, in the Krabi area of southern Thailand. Mountains and tropical rain forest surround it.
text.directions_text: No railway or tram stops serve this area, so from Krabi town head north-north-east to the temple grounds. The phone icon on the map is about 90 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the temple buildings and statues. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of mountains, trees and buildings. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details and for monkeys from a safe distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 90 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Face south-east, towards the temple, and take the first frames from here before walking on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the golden statue or the main building on one of the thirds. Include a few trees or the mountains behind to show the scale. At the top, the view over Krabi town works best with a strip of foreground, such as a railing or shrine roof, to add depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene, such as the golden statue, and slide the exposure down a little to keep detail in the gold. In shaded forest, tap on the subject and raise the exposure slightly. Wipe the lens first, as humidity can fog it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a sensible choice, as the climb is cooler and the crowds are likely smaller. Check the official site before you go for current opening arrangements.

text.access_note: This is a working Buddhist temple and meditation centre, so dress and behave respectfully, and check the official site before you go for access details.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is likely to be cooler and quieter for the climb.
Humidity can fog a phone lens.
Dressing respectfully is expected at a Buddhist temple.
Exposing for the bright golden statue helps keep detail in the gold.

label: Wat Kaew Korawaram

text.description: Wat Kaew Korawaram is a Buddhist temple on a hill above downtown Krabi Town, and one of the larger temples in the area. It is less famous than Wat Tham Suea (Tiger Cave Temple). You reach it from an entrance plaza off one of the town's main streets, then climb a grand staircase lined with naga (serpent) sculptures. The staircase leads the eye up the hill, and the white ordination hall sits at the top. From the terrace at the top you can turn round and look back over Krabi Town's rooftops to the Krabi River. That view makes a good wide photo, with the temple behind you as context. For a second angle, try Thanon Maharat. From there the white hall and the gold-railed staircase rise up the hill against the sky. This is a working temple, so keep to the posted rules and dress modestly. Photography is generally fine on the terrace and in the grounds, but the ordination hall has restrictions. Signs at the entrance say no professional photo shoots. Take your time on the way up, stop on the staircase for a few frames, and save the wide town view for the terrace.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Krabi Town, on a hill above the downtown area. The entrance plaza is off one of the town's main streets.
text.directions_text: Start from the middle of Krabi Town and head to the temple's entrance plaza off one of the main streets. From the plaza, climb the naga-lined staircase to the terrace at the top. That terrace is the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the town view from the terrace. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full staircase and the nagas. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out rooftops and the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face away from the white hall, looking back over the town toward the river. You get a wide view of Krabi Town's rooftops and the Krabi River, with the hall behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line so the rooftops and river fill the frame. Keep the phone level so the town doesn't tilt. For a different angle, the street called Thanon Maharat shows the white hall and gold-railed staircase rising up the hill against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the town or river to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. If you shoot the staircase from below with the ultra-wide, keep the phone upright to limit leaning lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sunset light softens the hills and town.

text.access_note: A working temple: dress modestly, follow the posted rules and expect restrictions at the ordination hall.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone upright when using the ultra-wide limits leaning vertical lines.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep colour in a bright sky.
Turning around at the top of the staircase puts the town and river in view, with the hall behind you (from the researched viewpoint notes).

name: Phra Nang Beach
label: Phra Nang Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Railay Viewpoint' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Railay Viewpoint Resort' (node/3419574714): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM R19741816 (Ao Phra Nang): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Famous beach below the cliffs at the tip of Railay.

text.description: Phra Nang Beach is a curved stretch of pale sand with a limestone cliff rising behind it, longtail boats on the water and a rock islet offshore. It photographs well because the beach, rock and sea all fit into one frame. The map's stand-here point is a high lookout rather than the sand. From up there you see Phra Nang Beach, Railay East and Railay West together, set among limestone karsts and mangroves. Guides describe it as the standout elevated view over Phra Nang, and it is a good alternative to shooting from the beach. The lookout is reached by the trail between Phra Nang Beach and Railay East. It is a steep, unmarked climb of about 25 minutes that some visitors find difficult, and it needs a scramble and a squeeze through a tunnel. Wear closed shoes and keep your phone in a pocket while you climb. If that sounds too much, the beach itself is a gentler option. The Bat Cave offers a framed view through its opening onto the beach and Ko Rang Nok island, but it is also a rock-climbing area, so keep out of climbers' way. Tides matter. One guide warns the beach may not be visible at high tide, while another recommends high tide for the Bat Cave view, so check the tide before you go. Whichever you choose, take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the scene changes a lot between a wide view and a close one.
text.geographic_location: Phra Nang Beach lies in the Railay area of Krabi, next to Railay East and Railay West. It has no road access, and the lookout sits on the trail between the beach and Railay East.
text.directions_text: Phra Nang has no road access. Boats land at Railay, and the last stretch to the beach is a walk of about 10 minutes from Railay East. For the lookout, take the trail between Railay East and Phra Nang Beach and allow about 25 minutes for the climb. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the beach, Railay East and Railay West in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cliffs, the rock islet or the longtail boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Railay Viewpoint (hilltop lookout reached by the trail between Phra Nang Beach and Railay East). A high overview of Phra Nang Beach, Railay East and Railay West set among the limestone karsts and mangroves. From here you look south-west over Phra Nang Beach, with Railay East and Railay West and the limestone karsts and mangroves around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the curve of the beach along a lower third line, with the karsts filling the upper part. Keep a few feet of foreground rock or trees at the edge to give a sense of height. If the climb is too much, shoot from the sand looking along the beach so the cliff rises behind the sand and water, or try the Bat Cave opening as a natural frame onto the beach.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or water to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale sand does not burn out. Wipe the lens before you shoot, and try a panorama to take in the full sweep of the bay.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Tides matter, so check the tide before you go: the beach may not be visible at high tide, while high tide is recommended for the Bat Cave view.

text.access_note: No paid viewpoints were recommended, but the climb is steep and rough and the Bat Cave is a climbing area, so check the official site or local information before you go.

name: Ko Poda
label: Koh Poda
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ko Poda Beach' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N5477098924 (Poda): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Island with white sand beach, popular on four-island boat tours.

text.description:
Ko Poda is a small island off the Krabi coast, and its northeast beach is the classic place for a holiday photo. White sand and turquoise water fill the foreground, and a tall limestone rock stands out of the sea just in front of the island. Guides describe that giant rock as the classic photo subject, and the rock formations along the beach make a popular backdrop. The same stretch of sand is also described as the best place on the island to swim, so you can combine the photos with a dip.

The view works well on a phone because it is simple: sand at the bottom, sea in the middle, rock rising behind. Stand on the beach, face the big rock, and let the shoreline lead the eye towards it. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) if you want to fit in the curve of the sand and the whole height of the rock. The default lens (1x) gives a calmer, more natural look. If you want the rock's texture, step back and use the telephoto (2x or more) instead of walking closer.

Sunset is the best moment, with the sun going down behind the rock formation. The beach is busy with tour groups from late morning until about 1-2 pm, so early or late visits give you cleaner shots with fewer people in the frame. If you want a quieter alternative, Secret Beach is a small bay with rock cliffs rising on both sides to frame the sea and sand. It is reached only by boat.
text.geographic_location: Ko Poda is an island just off the Krabi coast.
text.directions_text: Ko Poda is an island, so you reach it only by boat or tour; check with your tour operator or local boat services for the departure point and schedule. Once you land on the northeast beach, the phone icon on the map is on the sand and the big rock is directly in front of you, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in the sand, the sea and the full height of the rock. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the rock.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face the big limestone rock in front of the island. From here the photo shows the white sand and turquoise water in the foreground, with the tall rock standing out of the sea behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a lower or upper third line. Place the rock off-centre and let the curve of the shoreline lead towards it. A little wet sand in the foreground adds depth. If you want a different view, Secret Beach is a small, quiet bay where cliffs on both sides frame the sea and sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rock to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky and water keep their colour at sunset. Try a Live Photo for waves rolling in. Keep your lens clean, as sea spray and sunscreen smear easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset, when the sun goes down behind the rock formation. Tour groups are busiest from late morning until about 1-2 pm, so early or late is quieter.

text.access_note: This is a beach on an island reached by boat, so check the official site or your tour operator for access, boat times and any fees before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide, default and telephoto lenses suit the framing described, on a typical modern smartphone.
Sea spray and sunscreen can smear a phone lens.
Boat return times may limit how late you can stay for sunset, so check them before you go.
